meta.title: Arguments · the streetlights and the sick days

source.usage_note: Every argument, question, option and explanation composed for CAT OS. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: The opening bundle: one of each core kind — assumption, weaken, strengthen, inference, flaw, paradox — on everyday civic and workplace arguments, so the structure of an argument is the whole difficulty.

quality.adversarial_review: Item 1: the cost-effectiveness option is the rival for readers who confuse 'needed for the plan to be wise' with 'needed for the conclusion to follow'; the conclusion (lighting deters theft) needs no claim about cost. Item 4: the 'no member before twenty-five' option is the near-tie; it fails because a member could begin at seventeen and finish at twenty-one, which the premises allow. Item 6: the falling-motor-traffic option is tempting as an explanation but deepens the puzzle rather than resolving it.

items.argument: After the city council installed brighter streetlights in the market district, reported thefts there fell by a third within a year. The council concludes that brighter lighting deters theft, and it plans to extend the programme to every district in the city.
items.stem: The council's conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Of the measures open to the council, brighter lighting is the one that deters theft at the lowest cost.
options.B: Before the new lights, reported thefts in the market district had been rising rather than holding steady.
options.C: The fall in reported thefts was not mainly caused by some other change in the district during the same year.
options.D: Reported thefts in the market district fell in the year after the brighter lights were installed there.

premises: Brighter streetlights were installed in the market district.
Reported thefts there fell by a third within a year.
structure.conclusion: Brighter lighting deters theft (and will do so in every district).
structure.gap: That the lights, and not some other change in the same year, caused the fall — and that fewer reports means fewer thefts.

explanation.correct_reasoning: The argument moves from 'thefts fell after the lights' to 'the lights made thefts fall'. That step is only safe if nothing else explains the fall. Deny the correct option — suppose some other change did cause it — and the conclusion collapses, which is the test of a necessary assumption.

distractors.why_wrong: The conclusion is that lighting deters theft, not that it is the best buy among the options; the argument would stand even if some other measure open to the council deterred theft more cheaply.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like something a sensible council should believe before spending money.

distractors.why_wrong: Whether thefts were rising beforehand does not bear on whether the lights caused the fall; the argument compares before and after, not trend and after.
distractors.seductive_element: It supplies background that feels like it should matter to a before-and-after comparison.

distractors.why_wrong: This is one of the argument's stated premises; an assumption is something unstated that the argument needs, not something it already says.
distractors.seductive_element: It is certainly something the argument relies on — because the argument states it.

explanation.method: Write the argument as 'A happened, then B fell, so A caused B'. The necessary assumption is always the sentence that rules out the other ways B could have fallen. Confirm by negation: if the option were false, would the conclusion still follow?

items.argument: Employees who take part in the company's voluntary wellness programme take, on average, four fewer sick days a year than employees who do not. The company therefore proposes to make the programme compulsory, expecting the number of sick days across the whole workforce to fall.
items.stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the company's reasoning?

options.A: Employees who are already healthy and rarely take sick days are far more likely to volunteer than those in poor health.
options.B: Once enrolment is company-wide, the programme will cost less per employee each year than a single sick day costs.
options.C: Employees who complete the programme report feeling noticeably more energetic at work, whether or not they joined willingly.
options.D: At other companies, compulsory wellness programmes have left staff resentful of the management that imposed them.

premises: Volunteers for the programme take four fewer sick days a year than non-participants.
structure.conclusion: Making the programme compulsory will reduce sick days across the whole workforce.
structure.gap: That the programme causes the difference — rather than the kind of person who volunteers being different to begin with.

explanation.correct_reasoning: If the healthy volunteer and the unwell do not, the four-day gap is explained by who joins, not by what the programme does. Forcing everyone in would then add the unwell to the programme without changing their health, and sick days would not fall. This breaks the link between the evidence and the conclusion without denying the evidence.

distractors.why_wrong: The condition it offers is a financial one: even if compulsory enrolment left the programme cheaper per head than a day's absence, that bears on whether it is worth running, not on whether it causes sick days to fall.
distractors.seductive_element: It speaks to the very scale-up the proposal involves, which makes a financial fact feel like a verdict on the reasoning.

distractors.why_wrong: If the effect survives unwilling enrolment, the programme plausibly does something that compulsion would not destroy — which supports the causal story rather than undermining it.
distractors.seductive_element: It appears to answer the obvious worry about compulsion, and an option that meets that worry feels like the one under test.

distractors.why_wrong: Unpopularity is a different problem from ineffectiveness; the argument concludes that sick days will fall, and staff resentment does not show they will not.
distractors.seductive_element: It is a genuine reason to hesitate over the proposal, just not a reason to doubt the reasoning.

explanation.method: When an argument compares volunteers with non-volunteers, ask who volunteers. A difference between self-selected groups may have existed before the programme did; the weakener names that prior difference.

items.argument: Archaeologists argue that the settlement was abandoned suddenly rather than gradually. Their evidence is that household objects — pots, tools, even a loom with cloth still stretched on it — were left in place, whereas people who leave slowly carry their possessions away.
items.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the archaeologists' argument?

options.A: The pots and tools left in place were of a type in common use across the surrounding region for centuries beforehand.
options.B: A loom is large and awkward enough that even a household leaving over several months would have had to abandon it.
options.C: The settlement was abandoned in the same decade as a drought that the region's written sources record as lasting years.
options.D: Settlements known to have been abandoned gradually show a steady thinning of household objects in their latest layers.

premises: Household objects, including a loom with cloth on it, were left in place.
structure.conclusion: The settlement was abandoned suddenly rather than gradually.
structure.gap: That gradual abandonment really does leave fewer objects behind — the comparison the argument relies on but does not prove.

explanation.correct_reasoning: The argument rests on a contrast: sudden leavers abandon their things, gradual leavers take them. Evidence that gradually abandoned settlements do show thinning possessions confirms exactly that contrast, so objects left in place become stronger evidence of suddenness.

distractors.why_wrong: How widespread the type was, and for how long, helps date and place the settlement; it says nothing about why the objects were left, and the manner of leaving is what the argument is about.
distractors.seductive_element: Details about the objects feel like they should help an argument built on objects.

distractors.why_wrong: The condition it supplies covers the gradual case too: if even a household leaving over months would have abandoned the loom, finding one in place is compatible with a slow departure, which weakens the loom's value as evidence of suddenness.
distractors.seductive_element: It explains the loom, which was the argument's most striking detail.

distractors.why_wrong: A dated cause supports the claim that the settlement emptied, and perhaps why, but a drought the sources record as lasting years fits a gradual departure at least as well as a sudden one.
distractors.seductive_element: It supplies a cause, and causes feel like support for any conclusion about an event.

explanation.method: Find the comparison hidden in the argument ('unlike people who leave slowly…'). The strongest support is evidence that the comparison holds in known cases; the decoys support the wrong claim or explain away the evidence.

items.argument: Every member of the guild must have completed an apprenticeship of at least four years. Some members of the guild began their apprenticeships after the age of thirty. No apprenticeship can be completed before the age of twenty-one.
items.stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?

options.A: Some members of the guild were at least thirty-four years old when they became eligible to join.
options.B: Most members of the guild began their apprenticeships before thirty, and the rest not long after it.
options.C: No member became eligible before twenty-five, four years on from the minimum age of twenty-one.
options.D: Anyone who completes a four-year apprenticeship after the age of twenty-one may join the guild.

premises: Membership requires an apprenticeship of at least four years.
Some members began their apprenticeships after thirty.
structure.conclusion: What the three statements jointly force.

explanation.correct_reasoning: Take the members who began after thirty. Their apprenticeships lasted at least four years, so they finished after thirty-four; they could not have been eligible earlier. 'Some … at least thirty-four' follows with no extra assumption.

distractors.why_wrong: 'Some began after thirty' leaves the remainder unquantified, and is consistent with every other member having begun after thirty as well; both the 'most' and the timing of the rest are quantities the statements never supply.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like the natural complement of 'some began after thirty'.

distractors.why_wrong: The arithmetic it offers misreads the rule: twenty-one is the earliest an apprenticeship can be finished, not the earliest it can be begun, so an apprentice may start at seventeen and be eligible at twenty-one.
distractors.seductive_element: Adding four years to twenty-one gives twenty-five, which looks like arithmetic the premises support.

distractors.why_wrong: The statements make an apprenticeship a requirement for membership, not a qualification that confers it; attaching an age to the reversed condition does not repair the reversal.
distractors.seductive_element: It restates the first premise in the other direction, which reads almost the same.

explanation.method: For 'must be true', build the smallest case the premises allow and the largest, and see what holds in both. Watch every quantity word — 'some', 'most', 'no', 'at least' — because the distractors change exactly one of them.

items.argument: Critics of the new curriculum say that it lowers standards. But the same critics opposed the previous curriculum when it was introduced, and that curriculum is now widely praised. Their objection to the new curriculum can therefore be dismissed.
items.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to which of the following criticisms?

options.A: It assumes that the previous curriculum came to be praised because the same critics had opposed it at the time.
options.B: It fails to say what a 'standard' is, or how anyone could tell whether a given curriculum had lowered one.
options.C: It rejects an objection on the basis of who is making it, rather than by examining whether the objection is true.
options.D: It relies on the testimony of critics who have no special expertise in how a curriculum affects standards.

premises: The critics say the new curriculum lowers standards.
The same critics opposed the previous curriculum, which is now praised.
structure.conclusion: The critics' objection can be dismissed.
structure.gap: That being wrong before makes an objection wrong now — the objection itself is never examined.

explanation.correct_reasoning: The argument never engages with whether the new curriculum lowers standards. It dismisses the claim because of the critics' record — a fact about the people, not about the claim. That is the flaw: the truth of an objection does not depend on who raises it.

distractors.why_wrong: The argument makes no causal claim about why the previous curriculum is praised; it only notes that the critics opposed something now approved of.
distractors.seductive_element: It names a causal confusion, and causal confusions are common flaws.

distractors.why_wrong: Vagueness about 'standards' would be a weakness in the critics' claim, not in the argument's reasoning about how to treat that claim.
distractors.seductive_element: Definitions feel like a rigorous thing to demand.

distractors.why_wrong: The argument does not rely on the critics' testimony; it rejects it. And the critics' expertise is not the issue — an objection from a non-expert can still be true.
distractors.seductive_element: It stays with the critics, who are the argument's subject, and expertise sounds like a relevant test.

explanation.method: Ask what the conclusion is about (the objection) and what the evidence is about (the objectors). When the two differ, the flaw is usually that the argument judged the claim by its source.

items.argument: Over the past decade the town has doubled the length of its cycle lanes, yet the number of cyclists injured on its roads each year has risen sharply.
items.stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent contradiction?

options.A: Injuries to pedestrians have risen over the same decade, at much the same rate as injuries to cyclists.
options.B: The town's cycle lanes are separated from motor traffic and are regarded as among the best designed in the country.
options.C: Motor traffic has fallen considerably over the same period, and with it the number of collisions at junctions.
options.D: The new lanes have drawn many more people into cycling, so that bicycle journeys have more than doubled.

premises: Injuries to cyclists have risen sharply.
structure.conclusion: There is an apparent contradiction between safer infrastructure and more injuries.
structure.gap: The two facts are about different quantities: lanes and injuries, not the rate of injury per journey.

explanation.correct_reasoning: If bicycle journeys more than doubled, injuries could rise even while each journey became safer. Both facts stay true and stop conflicting: more lanes, more cyclists, more total injuries, a lower rate. A resolution keeps every fact and removes the tension.

distractors.why_wrong: A matching rise among pedestrians names no cause, so it relocates the puzzle rather than dissolving it; and pedestrians do not use the cycle lanes, which is the fact the rise has to be reconciled with.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like part of a wider pattern of rising injuries.

distractors.why_wrong: Lanes separated from traffic and admired for their design make the puzzle sharper, not clearer: the safer the infrastructure, the more surprising the rise in injuries.
distractors.seductive_element: It praises the lanes, which feels like it should reconcile them with something.

distractors.why_wrong: Fewer vehicles and fewer collisions at junctions should mean fewer injured cyclists, so this deepens the contradiction instead of resolving it.
distractors.seductive_element: It changes the traffic picture, and traffic feels like the obvious cause of injuries.

explanation.method: A paradox is two true facts that seem to clash. The resolution is a third fact that lets both stand — usually by revealing that they measure different things (a total against a rate, a group against a subgroup). Options that make one fact more surprising are the decoys.
